title: Injectable Biomaterial Travels Through Bloodstream to Mend Hearts from Within
summary: A revolutionary biomaterial that navigates the bloodstream to repair damaged organs could transform how we treat heart attacks and other inflammatory conditions. Developed by bioengineers at the University of California San Diego, the material is a powder that, when reconstituted with sterile water, forms a suspension of nanoparticles capable of homing in on injured tissue. 'This biomaterial allows for treating damaged tissue from the inside out,' said Karen Christman, professor of bioengineering and lead researcher. 'It's a new approach to regenerative engineering.' The work, published in Nature Biomedical Engineering, builds on Christman's earlier hydrogel—a scaffold derived from decellularized heart muscle, or extracellular matrix (ECM). That gel showed promise in a phase 1 clinical trial when injected directly into the heart via catheter, but the needle-based delivery posed risks if used immediately after a heart attack. The breakthrough came when first author Martin Spang processed the hydrogel's liquid precursor in a centrifuge, isolating nano-sized particles. After dialysis, sterile filtration, and freeze-drying, the resulting powder could be infused intravenously or through a coronary artery. The team expected the nanoparticles to slip through gaps that form between endothelial cells lining blood vessels after a heart attack. Instead, they observed something more surprising: the particles bound to those endothelial cells, helped close the gaps, and accelerated vascular healing. This reduced inflammation—a key driver of secondary tissue damage. In rodent and porcine models of acute myocardial infarction, intracoronary infusion led to reduced left ventricular volumes, improved wall motion scores, and gene expression shifts associated with repair. 'We sought to design a therapy that could be delivered to difficult-to-access organs,' Spang explained, 'and we came up with the method to take advantage of the bloodstream.' The material degrades within about three days, minimizing long-term risks. With an estimated 785,000 new heart attacks annually in the U.S. and no established therapy to directly repair cardiac tissue, this approach could fill a critical gap. Early experiments also hint at broader applications, including traumatic brain injury and pulmonary arterial hypertension. Human safety trials could begin within one to two years, offering hope that a simple infusion might one day heal hearts from the inside out.
why_it_matters: Heart disease remains the leading cause of death worldwide. A treatment that can be given through a simple IV drip to actually repair damaged heart muscle could save millions of lives and reduce disability. This research shows how clever engineering can turn a basic understanding of biology into a transformative medicine.

background_read: Heart attacks occur when a coronary artery is blocked, starving the heart muscle of oxygen and causing permanent damage. Current treatments can restore blood flow but do not repair the dead tissue, leaving patients with weakened hearts.

For over a decade, bioengineer Karen Christman (a professor at UC San Diego) has worked on a hydrogel made from the extracellular matrix of pig hearts—a material that provides structural support and signals to help cells regenerate.

An earlier version of the gel could only be delivered by needle directly into the heart wall, which was risky right after a heart attack. The new breakthrough, led by researcher Martin Spang, processed the hydrogel into nanoparticles small enough to be safely infused through the bloodstream.

These particles unexpectedly latched onto endothelial cells (the cells lining blood vessels), sealing leaky gaps and reducing dangerous inflammation. The results, published in Nature Biomedical Engineering, showed improved heart function in rats and pigs, and the team hopes human clinical trials can start within a couple of years.

perspectives.description: This approach could revolutionize cardiology by enabling regeneration without invasive surgery. For patients, it might mean better recovery after a heart attack and a lower risk of heart failure.

The therapy has only been tested in animals, and many promising treatments fail in human trials. The long-term effects of foreign particles binding to blood vessels are unknown, and manufacturing clinical-grade material could be costly and complex.

The research cleverly repurposes the body's own repair signals from extracellular matrix. It also highlights how unexpected results—like the particles sticking to endothelial cells—can lead to new understanding of healing mechanisms.

If human trials succeed, similar nanotechnology could be developed for stroke recovery, spinal cord injury, and even organ-on-a-chip applications. The challenge will be ensuring the particles go only where needed and do not cause unintended side effects.
